lead: A radar sees the echo a target returns, not its outline. Two objects of the same physical size can return echoes differing by a factor of ten thousand, because echo depends on shape, aspect angle and wavelength. Engineers describe a target by one number, radar cross section σ, an equivalent area in square metres. It sits in the range equation of 6.2 and sets how far a radar can see an object.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.2 for σ in the range equation, and Unit 2 for effective aperture and the receiving antenna.

blocks.text: A target intercepts incident power and reradiates it in many directions. Replace it by a fictitious area that takes the same power and reradiates equally in all directions. Choose that area so the echo density at the radar matches the real echo. That area is σ.

blocks.where: σ is radar cross section in square metres (m²); R is target-to-radar distance in m; S_back is echo power density at the radar in W/m²; S_inc is incident power density at the target in W/m². The factor 4πR² is the sphere area over which the equivalent isotropic reradiator spreads its power.

blocks.text: Turned around, S_back = S_inc σ / (4πR²). That is the target term in 6.2. The 1/R² is spreading loss on the return path.
σ spans many powers of ten, so it is often quoted in dBsm: σ(dBsm) = 10 log₁₀(σ / 1 m²). Thus 1 m² is 0 dBsm, 100 m² is 20 dBsm and 0.01 m² is −20 dBsm.
σ is not shadow area. A thin wire, plate edge or cavity can have σ far larger than its outline; a shaped body can have σ far smaller.
The metal sphere is the one target with an exact cross section. Let a be radius in m and λ wavelength in m; form ka = 2πa/λ, where k = 2π/λ is wavenumber in rad/m.

items: Rayleigh region, ka ≪ 1: sphere much smaller than a wavelength; σ grows as a⁶ and falls as λ⁴. Rain drops and insects live here, so weather radar uses short wavelength.
Resonance or Mie region, ka roughly 1: σ oscillates with peaks and nulls around the optical value; no simple formula holds.
Optical region, ka ≫ 1: σ = πa², the projected area, independent of wavelength. Large aircraft or ship at X band lies here for big smooth parts.

blocks.text: A flat metal plate broadside is the opposite extreme. Every point reradiates in phase, so fields add coherently and power grows as area squared.

blocks.where: A is plate area in m²; λ is wavelength in m. Valid only near normal incidence. The A² shows coherent addition; 1/λ² is the same factor that gives a large aperture antenna its gain.

blocks.text: A corner reflector is two or three mutually perpendicular metal plates. A wave bounces once from each plate and leaves almost parallel to the way it came, so a large cross section is available over a wide angle range. Small boats carry corner reflectors so marine radar sees them; calibration targets use them because σ is trusted.
A half-wave dipole at resonance has σ of order 0.86λ². A short dipole is far smaller and its σ drops quickly as the wire is shortened.

sections.h3: Aspect, fluctuation and hiding a target

blocks.text: σ depends on direction. A few degrees off broadside, a plate's σ falls by tens of decibels because the coherent sum now cancels. Real targets have flat panels, edges and cavities, so RCS swings wildly as they turn. This echo fluctuation is covered by the Swerling models in 6.8.
These are orders of magnitude only. The same target can change by 20 dB or more between bands and between nose-on and broadside.

Reduce σ by shaping, radar absorbing material and aspect control. Shaping removes flat panels and right angles, tilts vertical surfaces so the flash goes upward, and buries engine faces behind bends. Absorbing material turns the incident wave into heat in a lossy layer, but is usually narrow band or thick. Stealth combines these with reduced platform emission.
Polarisation matters. A flat plate returns the same polarisation; a dihedral corner rotates it by 90°, so receive polarisation changes echo.

spec.title: Meaning of radar cross section
spec.aria: Definition of cross section: a target takes power from the incident wave and reradiates it as if isotropically, so echo density at the radar is incident density times sigma divided by four pi R squared.

examples.question: A flat metal plate of area 1 m² is seen broadside by an X-band radar at 10 GHz. (a) Find σ in m² and dBsm. (b) A metal sphere has the same projected area of 1 m². Find its radius, ka, and σ at the same frequency. (c) Compare the echoes.
steps: Wavelength: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸ m/s) / (10 × 10⁹ Hz) = 0.03 m, the 3 cm X band.
Plate broadside: σ = 4πA²/λ² = (4π × (1 m²)²) / (0.03 m)² = 12.566 / (9 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.3963 × 10⁴ m².
Sphere with πa² = 1 m² gives a = √(1/π) = 0.564 m.
k = 2π/λ = 2π/0.03 = 209.4 rad/m, so ka = 209.4 × 0.564 = 118.2 ≫ 1. The sphere is in the optical region, so σ = πa² = 1.0 m², that is 0 dBsm.
Ratio: 13963 / 1.0 ≈ 1.4 × 10⁴. The plate returns more than ten thousand times the power of the sphere, although both present 1 m² of projected area.
examples.answer: The plate has σ ≈ 13963 m² (41.45 dBsm) and the sphere of radius 0.564 m has σ = 1.0 m² (0 dBsm); the plate's echo is about 1.4 × 10⁴ times stronger.
examples.check:
import math
A = 1.0
lam = 0.03
sigma_plate = 4*math.pi*A**2/lam**2
print(round(sigma_plate))
print(round(10*math.log10(sigma_plate), 2))
a = math.sqrt(1/math.pi)
print(round(a, 3))
ka = (2*math.pi/lam)*a
print(round(ka, 1))
print(round(math.pi*a**2, 2))

traps: Reading σ as physical area. A 1 m² plate gives about 14000 m² of cross section at one angle and almost nothing a few degrees away, so 'the target is 1 m²' is meaningless without band and aspect.
Carrying an RCS value from one frequency to another. The same aircraft nose may be in the resonance region on VHF and the optical region on X band, with very different σ.
Dropping the reference of a decibel. 0 dBsm means 1 m², not zero area; −20 dBsm is 0.01 m². Do not confuse dBsm (area) with dB (a pure ratio).
Using the flat-plate formula off broadside. σ = 4πA²/λ² holds only at normal incidence; tilted, the coherent sum collapses and the pattern shows narrow spikes.
Forgetting that σ assumes isotropic reradiation. Use the real bistatic pattern instead and the number depends on receiver direction, so it is no longer the same σ.

quiz.q: Define radar cross section and give its unit.
quiz.a: σ = 4πR²(S_back/S_inc), the equivalent area that, intercepting the incident power density and reradiating it isotropically, gives the observed echo density at the radar. Unit m², often quoted in dBsm relative to 1 m².

quiz.q: What is 0 dBsm, and what is 20 dBsm in m²?
quiz.a: 0 dBsm is 1 m². 20 dBsm is 100 m².

quiz.q: Why does a broadside flat plate have much larger σ than a sphere of the same projected area?
quiz.a: The plate reradiates in phase over its whole area, so fields add coherently and power grows as A², giving σ = 4πA²/λ². The sphere scatters in many directions with phase varying over its curved surface, so no such coherent flash forms and σ stays near πa².

quiz.q: A metal sphere of radius 10 cm is seen by a 3 GHz radar. Find ka, the region, and σ.
quiz.a: λ = c/f = 0.1 m; k = 2π/λ = 62.8 rad/m; ka = 62.8 × 0.1 = 6.28, at the upper end of the Mie/resonance region. σ is close to, but not exactly, the optical value; σ ≈ πa² = 0.0314 m² (−15 dBsm) is a good approximation. Exact optical σ = πa² with no ripple needs ka ≫ 1.

quiz.q: A flat plate of area 0.5 m² is seen broadside at 3 GHz. Find σ in m² and dBsm.
quiz.a: λ = 0.1 m. σ = 4πA²/λ² = 4π(0.25)/0.01 = 314.2 m². In decibels: 10 log₁₀(314.2) = 25.0 dBsm.

quiz.q: An aircraft shows a strong echo nose-on and a weak one from the side. Give two reasons and one design change that reduces both.
quiz.a: Aspect changes which flat panels and edges are broadside, and the coherent sum can add or cancel; projected area also changes with aspect. Shaping removes flat panels and right angles by tilting surfaces and burying engine faces, and radar absorbing material lowers specular returns from all aspects.

quiz.q: A small drone is detected easily by X-band radar but poorly by VHF radar. Explain using the Rayleigh region.
quiz.a: At VHF the wavelength is metres long, so the drone has ka ≪ 1 and lies in the Rayleigh region, where σ falls as a⁶/λ⁴ — a few metres of wavelength makes σ very small. At X band (3 cm) the same drone has ka of order 1 to 10 and returns far more. This is why long-wavelength radars are used against small low-observable targets.

quiz.q: Why does a corner reflector return a large echo over a wide range of angles, while a flat plate does not?
quiz.a: The wave bounces off each of the mutually perpendicular plates in turn and leaves almost parallel to the incident direction, so the coherent return survives large changes of aspect. A single plate returns strongly only near broadside.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real RCS work is mostly computational: method of moments for wires, physical optics and shooting-and-bouncing rays for large platforms, full-wave solvers for cavities. Stealth combines these with absorbing material design and with managing infrared and visual signature. Bistatic and multistatic radar, with transmitter and receiver apart, spoils the single monostatic σ assumption. Search 'RCS prediction physical optics', 'Swerling models' and 'Jaumann layer' for more.
